title: The Instructional Hierarchy
author: fivetwelvethirteen
summary: The Instructional Hierarchy is a three-stage framework for developing math fact fluency: acquisition (accurate understanding through varied strategies), fluency (increasing speed through practice), and generalization (flexible application in new contexts). The framework resolves the timed-practice debate by clarifying that timed practice is appropriate in the fluency stage but counterproductive in the acquisition stage, where working memory overload produces errors, avoidance behaviors, and minimal actual practice. The core classroom challenge is that students across all three stages coexist in every class, making full differentiation the obvious but time-intensive solution. The author's practical alternative is to break multiplication facts into smaller chunks—one fact family at a time—so acquisition is solidified before fluency practice begins, avoiding the demotivating 'drill and kill' experience for students who aren't yet ready. The key diagnostic is watching the students who most need practice: if they are getting discouraged or working too slowly to accumulate reps, the practice has outpaced their acquisition. Mixing in generalization tasks keeps advanced students engaged during whole-class sessions without requiring separate tracks.
points: The Instructional Hierarchy's three stages—acquisition, fluency, generalization—clarify why timed fact practice is appropriate for fluent students but harmful for those still in the acquisition phase.
Premature fluency practice causes working memory overload, slow error-prone work, avoidance behaviors, and less actual practice for the students who most need it.
The practical solution is to work one fact family at a time, completing acquisition before beginning fluency practice, rather than attempting to differentiate across all stages simultaneously.
The most useful classroom diagnostic is watching whether the students who most need practice are getting discouraged or disengaged—a signal that chunks need to be broken down further.
quotes: Acquisition: Students learn math facts by connecting new facts to what they already know. The goal is to answer accurately but using a range of strategies, without an emphasis on speed.
In the acquisition stage, timed practice isn't appropriate. The goal is to get students calculating accurately and connecting what they're learning to what they already know.

This is the core challenge of fact fluency. If I'm working with a student one-on-one, the instructional hierarchy is really useful! In a classroom with a wide range of students, the reality is much more complicated.
Repetitive practice is most useful when students are in the fluency stage. Asking students to practice something while they are still in the acquisition stage is going to be inefficent.

I've seen this over and over again: students are trying to practice something but their working memory is overwhelmed, their work is slow and error-prone, the practice isn't very productive, and the whole experience is unpleasant for students.
Breaking facts into smaller chunks avoids excessive, repetitive practice before students are ready for it.
